# In-World Texts — Koans, Fables, Apocrypha

The quotable corpus: material the narrator can read at a remove in cold opens and
outros ([[narrator-framing]]). Each specimen carries its own status. Diegetic file:
everything here must pass the banned-vocabulary scan.

## The Fable of the Iron and the Thread

> status: provisional (D-0045)

*"They say the Mountain of Chalk grew tired of holding up the sky, so it asked the
Valley for a pillar of iron. The Valley gave its iron. The Keep built its pillar. But
the heavier the iron became, the faster the sky fell, until the clouds dragged
through the mud. The Arch-Scribes calculated the weight of the sky, but they forgot
to calculate the weight of the pillar. It was only when a beggar tied a single,
hollow reed to the peak that the sky remembered how to float. A ledger can measure
gravity, but only an empty vessel can hold the wind."*

## The Apocrypha of the Eaten Word

> status: provisional (D-0045, D-0046, D-0220)

*"A starving man asked the Scriptorium for bread. The Scribe, bound by the Ledger,
wrote the word 'Wheat' on a pristine piece of vellum and handed it to the man. The
man ate the vellum and died of Wyrd-rot. The Scribe was not punished for murder. He
was executed for wasting ink on a corpse. The Ledger prized the word it had written
above the hunger it refused to see. A clean account could be carried past a dead man
without acquiring his weight. To survive the Ledger, you must learn to eat the dirt."*

(Amended per D-0046: the original draft's final lines used a modern word; "the
Ledger" replaces it.)

## The Lesson of the False Measurement

> status: proposed

*"The Scribe asked the Skald: If the Wyrd is a river, how do you prove the water? The
Skald replied: You do not prove the water. You prove the thirst of the deer that
drinks from it. The Scribe, angered, dammed the river to measure its depth in still
iron. The water became a ledger. The deer died of thirst. And the river, possessing
no proof of its own existence, vanished into Wyrd-fog. Here ends the lesson of the
False Measurement. To name a thing without needing it is the genesis of all rot."*

## The Paradox of the Floating Quarry

> status: proposed

*"When the Keep of the Valley demanded iron, the miners stripped the mountain's
bones. But the mountain did not weep. It simply forgot the treaty of gravity. A stone
that forgets it is heavy will fall upward; a man who forgets he is a guest will be
swallowed by the sky. Thus began the paradox of the Floating Quarry."*

(An earlier-style specimen; superseded in manner by the more impenetrable koan form
the author requested in D-0045 — kept as a fable-register example.)

## Aphorisms of the three creeds
> status: proposed

Repeated creed-phrases the three faiths use as callbacks and value-orientation — the
heard medium's substitute for a visible holy symbol. Grouped by culture; each carries a
one-line note on how it is used. None is ratified.

**The empire's scribes.**

- *"The Ledger balances."* — The chilling all-purpose justification: whatever was taken,
  the reckoning required it. Spoken the way a clean hand washes itself of a verdict.
- *"Ink over earth."* — A creed of supremacy: the written count outranks the living
  Wyrd. The motto of enclosure.
- *"Nothing uncounted, nothing unbound."* — A scribe's valediction and quiet threat; to
  be off the rolls is to be prey.

**The native animists.**

- *"The Wyrd remembers the weight."* — Ecological debt: every taking is recorded by the
  world itself and comes due. Both comfort and warning.
- *"No knot tied alone."* — The organizing line of the whole creed: magic and survival
  are shared, never solitary; mutual aid stated as folk wisdom.
- *"Leave the root, take the fruit."* — The rule of sustainable harvest, taught to
  children before they can reason a proof.

**The working poor.**

- *"Keep your head below the mist."* — Survival by going unnoticed; precisely the fearful
  habit the protagonist must unteach the apprentice.
- *"Cold iron pays the toll."* — When high reasoning fails, grounded physical reality
  keeps you alive; trust the ground under your feet over any clever word.

Two questions the creeds raise are recorded, not resolved: which native line the
protagonist forces the apprentice to repeat before her first proof, and how heavily
each creed leans on its aphorisms from region to region — matters for [[religion]] and
[[audio-design]] to settle.
